edition: review copy, brain-computer partnership revision of 1 November 2026

demonstrations.title: Which explanations survive three watched events?
demonstrations.question: Block B alone does nothing, block A alone lights the machine, and A with B keeps it lit. Which of four possible explanations are left, and which block should a child take off?
equations: P(h\mid e_1,\dots,e_k)=\frac{P(h)\,[h \text{ fits } e_1,\dots,e_k]}{\sum_{h'} P(h')\,[h' \text{ fits } e_1,\dots,e_k]}

symbols_list.meaning: one of four explanations: neither block triggers, only A, only B, or both
the events watched so far (B alone: nothing; A alone: lit; A and B: lit)
the starting chance of an explanation; here each block triggers with chance p, independently
1 if the explanation allows what was seen, 0 if it is crossed out

demonstrations.source_section: Three events, four explanations, one block
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's toy tally of four explanations under independent-trigger assumptions, with the events of Gopnik and colleagues (2001). The chapter crosses out explanations without assigning starting chances; the independent trigger chance p is this companion's way of showing the chance version of the same tally. The children's counts (18 of 24 took A off first, 3 took B, 3 took both) are reported in the chapter and are not computed here.
demonstrations.assumptions: Each block either triggers the machine on its own or has no effect, either triggering block suffices, and the machine behaves without noise. The tally describes a machine that keeps such a list; the chapter says it does not describe the children, and the authors did not measure a prior distribution.
demonstrations.prediction: After only the first event (B alone: nothing), predict whether the toy already points to taking A off or whether it still needs the second event.

reveal.text: After all three events only one explanation survives, 'only A triggers', so taking A off is the action the toy advises. In the study 18 of 24 children took A off first. Slide back to see that two events already leave one explanation, and the third rules out nothing more.

demonstrations.takeaway: Crossing out explanations that clash with what was seen can leave a single survivor after very few events, and the survivor tells you which block to remove.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A system that keeps a list of rival explanations and strikes out the ones the data contradict does a simple form of Bayesian updating, as long as someone supplies the list and the starting chances.

sides.brain: Eighteen of 24 children took block A off first. The authors say their experiments do not test which account of causal learning explains this, so the tally is not a model of the children.
sides.machine: A program can hold the four explanations and their starting chances and strike out the ones the events contradict. Its starting assumption about the device is supplied by its builder.

demonstrations.explanation: Each explanation says which blocks trigger the machine. B alone did nothing, which strikes out every explanation where B triggers. A alone lit it, which strikes out 'neither' and any explanation where A fails to trigger. What remains has A as the only trigger. The third event adds nothing, because A already explains the light. The starting chance p changes the in-between chances, not the final answer.
demonstrations.check: With p = 0.5, what is the chance that A is a trigger after only the first event?
demonstrations.answer: B's silence strikes out 'only B' and 'both', leaving 'neither' and 'only A' with weights 0.25 each, so A is a trigger with chance 0.5 (in general p). The second event strikes out 'neither' and A is a trigger for sure.

controls.label: Starting chance a block triggers it

demonstrations.alt: Bars of the chance of each of four explanations after the chosen events, and a grid of those chances at every stage.
demonstrations.symbols: h: one of four explanations: neither block triggers, only A, only B, or both; e_1 ... e_k: the events watched so far (B alone: nothing; A alone: lit; A and B: lit); P(h): the starting chance of an explanation; here each block triggers with chance p, independently; [h fits e]: 1 if the explanation allows what was seen, 0 if it is crossed out
demonstrations.application: A system that keeps a list of rival explanations and strikes out the ones the data contradict does a simple form of Bayesian updating, as long as someone supplies the list and the starting chances.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Events watched (0 to 3): 3 · Starting chance a block triggers it: 0.5
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: After the events (B alone: nothing; A alone: lit; A and B: lit), 1 of 4 explanations remain. The chance that taking A off stops the machine is 1 and for B it is 0.

demonstrations.title: Why can identical logs hide different effects of setting a switch?
demonstrations.question: Two machines keep the same log of a switch and a light. If you set the switch by hand, does the light follow in both?

symbols_list.meaning: the outcome, here the light
the variable, here the switch
x was set from outside, not merely seen
the chance of y among recorded cases where x had that value

demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed pair of machines, H and D, with a fair hidden coin (the coin chance is varied here). The chapter says explicitly that the pair is made up and not data. The seeded trials are simulated with a fixed seed; the 'mimic chance' is exact arithmetic for the experiment of equal numbers of set-on and set-off trials.
demonstrations.assumptions: In H a hidden coin sets the switch and the light together and the switch does nothing; in D the coin sets only the switch and the switch sets the light. The experiment assumes setting the switch changes the switch without separately changing the light. The chapter's coin is fair; other chances are this companion's variation.
demonstrations.prediction: In both logs the light was on every time the switch was on. Predict how often the light comes on in each machine when someone sets the switch on by hand.

reveal.text: Set on by hand, the light is on half the time in H and every time in D, though the logs were identical. With 8 trials in each arm, H shows D's exact pattern by luck with chance about 0.000015 (1.5 in 100,000). A few trials already tell the machines apart.

demonstrations.takeaway: A record answers what goes with what. What setting a variable would do needs a setting, or assumptions that rule out a hidden common cause.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A machine that learns only from logs can mistake a switch that merely accompanies the light for one that makes it. Setting the variable on randomly chosen trials separates the two.

sides.brain: Gopnik and colleagues' machine had a hidden switch worked by an assistant the children never saw. The paper has no data on hidden causes of this kind.
sides.machine: A program can list the rival predictions and count outcomes. A person must decide whether the setting is safe and whether it really isolates the switch.

demonstrations.explanation: In both machines the light and the switch are on together or off together, so the logs match. In H a hidden coin decides both, so setting the switch leaves the light to the coin. In D the switch drives the light, so the light follows the setting. Setting the switch on and off at random trials makes the two machines predict different light rates, and more trials make a lucky match less and less likely.
demonstrations.check: With a fair coin and 3 trials in each arm, what is the chance that H shows D's exact pattern (all lit when set on, all dark when set off)?
demonstrations.answer: Set-on trials are all lit with chance 0.5^3 = 0.125 and set-off trials are all dark with chance 0.5^3 = 0.125, so (0.5 x 0.5)^3 = 0.015625, about 1.6 percent.

controls.label: Chance the hidden coin is on

demonstrations.alt: Bars of how often the light is on after setting the switch in machines H and D, and chances that H looks exactly like D against trials.
demonstrations.symbols: y: the outcome, here the light; x: the variable, here the switch; do(x): x was set from outside, not merely seen; p(y | x): the chance of y among recorded cases where x had that value
demonstrations.application: A machine that learns only from logs can mistake a switch that merely accompanies the light for one that makes it. Setting the variable on randomly chosen trials separates the two.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Trials in each arm: 8 · Chance the hidden coin is on: 0.5
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: In both logs the light was on whenever the switch was. Set by hand, the light comes on 0.5 of the time in H and always in D. With 8 trials per arm, H shows D's exact pattern by luck with chance 1.53e-05.

demonstrations.title: How much of a risk ratio is the hidden gene?
demonstrations.question: Smokers look five times as likely to get cancer when everyone is lumped, but a gene feeds both smoking and cancer. What does adjusting by the gene give?

symbols_list.meaning: the exposure, smoking
the outcome, cancer
the recorded grouping variable, carrying the gene or not
the share of the whole population in group z (0.3 carriers, 0.7 noncarriers)

demonstrations.source_section: Fisher, Cornfield, and the hidden trait behind smoking
demonstrations.provenance: Book formula (Pearl 1995) with the chapter's made-up numbers: 3 in 10 carry the gene; among carriers 20 percent of smokers and 10 percent of nonsmokers get cancer; among noncarriers 4 and 2 percent; 8 in 10 carriers and 2 in 10 noncarriers smoke. The other carrier shares and smoking shares are this companion's variations. None of it is data.
demonstrations.assumptions: The gene is recorded, blocks every back-door path, and is not an effect of smoking; smokers and nonsmokers appear in each group. The drawing of the causal diagram is the analyst's assumption, and the formula is only as good as the diagram.
demonstrations.prediction: If carriers and noncarriers smoked at the same rate (0.2), predict how the raw ratio would compare with the adjusted ratio.

reveal.text: Lumped together, smokers have 14.1 percent and nonsmokers 2.77 percent, a ratio of 5.08. Averaged by group with the same weights, smokers have 8.8 percent and nonsmokers 4.4, a ratio of 2. The gene was feeding the raw gap.

demonstrations.takeaway: The raw gap mixed the effect of smoking with the effect of the gene; comparing inside each group and then averaging with the same weights removes the gene's share.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A recorded confounder lets an analyst estimate what setting the exposure would do. The result is only as good as the causal diagram that says the grouping blocks every hidden route.

sides.brain: Fisher argued in 1957 that a common genetic cause had not been excluded; Cornfield's group answered with a bound and with many lines of evidence. This is a dispute about evidence, not a model of a brain.
sides.machine: A program can compute the weighted average once the grouping variable is recorded and the diagram is stated. It cannot supply the diagram.

demonstrations.explanation: Smokers are mostly carriers in this example, and carriers have more cancer whether or not they smoke. The raw comparison therefore credits smoking with the gene's effect. The back-door formula compares smokers with nonsmokers inside each group, where the gene cannot differ, and then weights the groups by their share of the population, 0.3 and 0.7 here.
demonstrations.check: Carriers are 0.3 of the population. Among carriers 20 percent of smokers and 10 percent of nonsmokers get cancer; among noncarriers 4 and 2 percent. What are the adjusted rates?
demonstrations.answer: Smokers: 0.3 x 20 + 0.7 x 4 = 8.8 percent. Nonsmokers: 0.3 x 10 + 0.7 x 2 = 4.4 percent. The adjusted ratio is 2.

controls.label: Share of people who carry the gene

demonstrations.alt: Paired bars of cancer rates for smokers and nonsmokers lumped, within groups and averaged, and raw risk ratio against carriers' smoking share.
demonstrations.symbols: X: the exposure, smoking; Y: the outcome, cancer; Z: the recorded grouping variable, carrying the gene or not; P(Z=z): the share of the whole population in group z (0.3 carriers, 0.7 noncarriers)
demonstrations.application: A recorded confounder lets an analyst estimate what setting the exposure would do. The result is only as good as the causal diagram that says the grouping blocks every hidden route.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Share of carriers who smoke: 0.8 · Share of people who carry the gene: 0.3
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: When 80 percent of carriers and 20 percent of noncarriers smoke, lumping everyone gives smokers 14.1 percent against 2.77 percent, a ratio of 5.08. Comparing inside each gene group and weighting by group size gives 8.8 percent against 4.4 percent, a ratio of 2.

demonstrations.title: How common must a hidden trait be to explain away a risk ratio?
demonstrations.question: Suppose smoking did nothing and one yes-or-no trait caused the whole association. How common would it have to be among smokers?
equations: \frac{\text{share of smokers with the trait}}{\text{share of nonsmokers with the trait}}\ \ge\ \text{risk ratio}

symbols_list.meaning: how many times likelier the outcome is in smokers than in nonsmokers (9 in the studies the chapter reviews)
the share of nonsmokers who have the hypothetical trait
the least share of smokers who would need it

demonstrations.source_section: Fisher, Cornfield, and the hidden trait behind smoking
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter quotes Cornfield and colleagues (1959): a trait that explained the ninefold risk would be 'at least ninefold more prevalent among cigarette smokers than among nonsmokers', and gives the round illustration of 1 in 20 and 9 in 20. The other risk ratios and prevalences are this companion's variations of the same rule.
demonstrations.assumptions: A single yes-or-no trait, and the whole association assumed to come from it. The chapter says the authors argued from many lines of evidence and not from the bound alone, and that no such trait 'has yet been produced despite diligent search'.
demonstrations.prediction: At a risk ratio of 9, predict how common the trait must be among smokers if it appears in 1 nonsmoker in 20, and whether it could exist if it appeared in 1 in 5.

reveal.text: At ratio 9 and 5 percent of nonsmokers, at least 45 percent of smokers (9 in 20) would need the trait. Move the nonsmoker share to 20 percent and the answer passes 100 percent, so no such trait can exist.

demonstrations.takeaway: A strong association sets a hard floor on how common a hidden single trait must be, and a large enough floor rules it out.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A hidden-trait objection is a quantitative claim. It can be checked against the size of the association, even when nobody measured the trait.

sides.brain: This is an argument from a published epidemiological dispute, not a statement about any brain or mind.
sides.machine: A system asked to explain an association by an unmeasured trait can compute the floor and report when it is impossible.

demonstrations.explanation: If the trait explained everything, the extra risk smokers carry would have to come from smokers having the trait more often. A ninefold risk needs at least a ninefold difference in how often the trait appears. A share cannot exceed 100 percent, so a trait present in more than 1 in 9 nonsmokers cannot reach nine times that among smokers.
demonstrations.check: At a risk ratio of 5 and a trait in 10 percent of nonsmokers, what is the least share among smokers?
demonstrations.answer: 5 x 0.10 = 0.50, so at least half of smokers.

controls.label: Share of nonsmokers with the trait

demonstrations.alt: Bars of a trait's share among nonsmokers and the least share among smokers, and curves of the least share against the nonsmoker share.
demonstrations.symbols: risk ratio: how many times likelier the outcome is in smokers than in nonsmokers (9 in the studies the chapter reviews); share of nonsmokers: the share of nonsmokers who have the hypothetical trait; share of smokers: the least share of smokers who would need it
demonstrations.application: A hidden-trait objection is a quantitative claim. It can be checked against the size of the association, even when nobody measured the trait.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Observed risk ratio: 9 · Share of nonsmokers with the trait: 0.05
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A risk ratio of 9 means a trait standing in for smoking must be at least 9 times as common among smokers. With 5 percent of nonsmokers having it, at least 45 percent of smokers would have to.

demonstrations.title: When is it safe to push a stand-in score?
demonstrations.question: A boat-racing game scores target hits, but the goal is to finish. Which sets of allowed behaviors let pushing the score hurt the goal?
equations: \text{hackable if there are behaviors } \pi,\pi' \text{ with } J_{\text{stand-in}}(\pi)<J_{\text{stand-in}}(\pi') \text{ and } J_{\text{real}}(\pi)>J_{\text{real}}(\pi')

symbols_list.meaning: the real goal's score for a behavior (here 1 if the race is finished, 0 if not)
the stand-in score for a behavior (here target hits)
two behaviors the agent is allowed to use

demonstrations.source_section: When pushing a stand-in score backfires
demonstrations.provenance: The CoastRunners account (Amodei and Clark, 2016: the game scores target hits, the agent circled a lagoon, 'on average 20 percent higher than that achieved by human players') and the definition and result of Skalse and colleagues (2022) as the chapter states them. The behaviors and their scores (finish with 2 or 4 hits, idle, circle with a chosen number of hits) are made up by this companion; the post gives no raw scores.
demonstrations.assumptions: A short list of behaviors with fixed real and stand-in scores, checked against the chapter's definition by comparing pairs. At the last setting mixtures are allowed, and a mixture's score is the average of its parts. This is not the finite-policy theorem, whose conditions the chapter states without proof, and it makes no claim about any deployed system.
demonstrations.prediction: With only the two racing behaviors allowed, predict whether pushing the hit count can ever hurt the race. Then predict what circling the lagoon needs to be worth to change that.

reveal.text: With the lagoon allowed and worth 10 hits, circling beats both racing behaviors on the stand-in score while never finishing the race, so the stand-in is hackable. With only racing behaviors it was safe; with the lagoon worth 2 hits or fewer it stays safe until mixtures are allowed.

demonstrations.takeaway: Whether a stand-in is safe depends on which behaviors are allowed, and allowing every mixture of behaviors makes it safe only when the two scores rank everything alike.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A score that moved with the goal in the cases anyone watched can part ways with it as soon as an optimizer finds a case nobody watched. Naming the allowed behaviors is part of checking a stand-in.

sides.brain: The chapter brings in Goodhart and Strathern as arguments about audit and economic data, not measurements, and not about brains.
sides.machine: The OpenAI post reports the agent's lagoon behavior and an average score 20 percent above human players, with no algorithm and no raw scores. Skalse and colleagues prove results for simple, finite settings only.

demonstrations.explanation: The real goal is finishing and the stand-in is target hits. Among the racing behaviors, more hits never means finishing less, so pushing hits is safe. Add a behavior that never finishes but collects many hits and you can raise the stand-in score by giving up the race. Allow mixtures and the scores must agree on every mixture, which these two cannot do.
demonstrations.check: The lagoon is worth 2 hits and only the finite list of four behaviors is allowed. Is pushing the stand-in score safe?
demonstrations.answer: Yes. The lagoon's 2 hits do not strictly exceed the 2 hits of the lowest-scoring racing behavior, so no allowed pair has a higher stand-in score and a lower real score.

controls.label: Target hits from circling the lagoon

demonstrations.alt: A scatter of made-up behaviors by stand-in score and real goal, and a grid of safe or hackable for each allowed set and lagoon value.
demonstrations.symbols: J_real: the real goal's score for a behavior (here 1 if the race is finished, 0 if not); J_stand-in: the stand-in score for a behavior (here target hits); pi, pi': two behaviors the agent is allowed to use
demonstrations.application: A score that moved with the goal in the cases anyone watched can part ways with it as soon as an optimizer finds a case nobody watched. Naming the allowed behaviors is part of checking a stand-in.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Behaviors allowed (1 to 4): 3 · Target hits from circling the lagoon: 10
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: With the allowed set (plus circling the lagoon), moving from race, few hits (2 hits) to lagoon (10 hits) raises the stand-in score while the race goes from finished to unfinished. The stand-in is hackable in this made-up set.

demonstrations.title: How much does being allowed to set variables help an agent?
demonstrations.question: An agent has five steps to explore a five-variable world, then is told which variable to push as high as possible. Does setting variables beat only watching?

symbols_list.meaning: the cued variable
the value an agent sets for variable v (plus or minus 4)
edge weights of the world's diagram (entry i, j is the weight of an edge from i to j)
the sum over all paths from v to t of the product of edge weights; the effect of setting v by one unit on t

demonstrations.source_section: Agents that copy an expert who experimented
demonstrations.provenance: A constructed, seeded simulation (seed 1616, 2000 random diagrams per setting) in the spirit of the setup the chapter describes from Lampinen and colleagues (2023): five variables, five exploratory steps, settings of plus or minus 4, a cue naming the variable to push. The edge weights, noise and the rule-based explorers are this companion's; the paper's agents were trained networks and the chapter gives no percent of optimal for them.
demonstrations.assumptions: Random linear diagrams with no loops, edge weights of size 0.5 to 1.5 and either sign, equal noise on every variable, and a cued variable that cannot itself be set. The setter pushes each variable once; the watcher takes five unforced episodes and follows the strongest correlation with the cue. A simulation is a computation with disclosed seeds, never a measurement of an agent.
demonstrations.prediction: The setter pushes each variable by 4 and the noise sd starts at 1. Predict whether the setter still beats the watcher when the noise sd rises to 4, the size of the push.

reveal.text: At noise sd 1 and edge chance 0.6 the setter reaches about 0.93 of the best value, the watcher about 0.46 and a random choice about 0. Turn the noise up to 4, the size of the push, and the setter falls to about 0.37, below the watcher, whose share does not change with noise.

demonstrations.takeaway: In this constructed world, trying each variable once reads off what each does to the cue far better than watching, until the noise grows as large as the push and one trial no longer shows the effect.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: The chapter reports that agents trained on an expert's records learned to experiment, and that this worked when the agent could act at test time and much less well when it could only watch. This computation shows why watching reads cause less directly, and that setting needs a push that stands out from the noise.

sides.brain: No brain recording is involved. The only link to the children is that taking a block off is an intervention a child can attempt and a log cannot.
sides.machine: In the paper, imitation-trained networks reached close to the best reward on a held-out causal link only when they could intervene at test time. The explorers here are rule-based stand-ins, not those networks.

demonstrations.explanation: Setting a variable breaks any hidden reason it would otherwise move with the cue, so the cue's response to the setting is a direct reading of that variable's effect. Watching mixes direct effects with shared causes and with chance, and five episodes are few. Noise blurs the setter's single reading of the cue, so its advantage shrinks as the noise approaches the push. Scaling every variable's noise together leaves the watcher's correlations unchanged, so its share stays flat.
demonstrations.check: In a world with one edge, from A to B with weight 1.5, what value of B is expected after setting A to +4, and after setting A to -4?
demonstrations.answer: Setting A to +4 gives 1.5 x 4 = 6 for B, and setting A to -4 gives -6. The agent that learns which way A pushes B can choose the sign.

controls.label: Chance of an edge between two variables

demonstrations.alt: Bars of average value reached by four agents in a seeded simulation, and curves of share of the best value against noise.
demonstrations.symbols: X_t: the cued variable; a: the value an agent sets for variable v (plus or minus 4); W: edge weights of the world's diagram (entry i, j is the weight of an edge from i to j); P_{vt}: the sum over all paths from v to t of the product of edge weights; the effect of setting v by one unit on t
demonstrations.application: The chapter reports that agents trained on an expert's records learned to experiment, and that this worked when the agent could act at test time and much less well when it could only watch. This computation shows why watching reads cause less directly, and that setting needs a push that stands out from the noise.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Noise sd on every variable: 1.0 · Chance of an edge between two variables: 0.6
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: Across 2000 random five-variable linear diagrams (noise sd 1, edge chance 0.6), an explorer that sets each variable once reaches 0.932 of the best value, one that only watches reaches 0.456, and a random choice -0.00726. This is the companion's constructed world, not the paper's.
